"Conceit" has two completely separate meanings that are used in different contexts. One is everyday, and one is literary. Understanding both will give you the full picture.
Meaning 1: An Inflated, Unrealistic Opinion of Yourself

This is the meaning you're most likely to encounter in daily life.

When someone has conceit, it means they think they are far more talented, intelligent, attractive, or important than they actually are. It goes beyond ordinary confidence. A confident person believes in themselves based on honest self-awareness. A person full of conceit has puffed up their own image in their mind — they are in love with themselves, and it shows.

Think of it this way: confidence says "I am good at this." Conceit says "I am the best, and everyone else is lesser."

Examples in use:

  • "His conceit was astonishing — he truly believed no one in the room was as smart as him."
  • "She had the talent, but her conceit drove away everyone who could have helped her."

The key adjective to know: Someone who has conceit is described as conceited. If someone calls you conceited, they mean you are arrogantly, unrealistically full of yourself. "Conceit" is the state; "conceited" is the quality.

Shades and nuance: Conceit carries a slightly old-fashioned and literary feel compared to the more casual word "arrogance." Arrogance often feels loud and aggressive — the arrogant person asserts their superiority. Conceit is more internal and self-absorbed — the conceited person is simply besotted with themselves. They may not even bother to attack others; they're too busy admiring themselves. It also overlaps with vanity, but vanity tends to focus specifically on physical appearance, while conceit is broader — it can apply to intelligence, skill, status, or any quality a person might overvalue in themselves.
Meaning 2: A Literary Device — An Elaborate, Surprising Comparison

This meaning lives in the world of literature and poetry, and it is completely unrelated to pride.

In writing — especially in poetry — a conceit is an extended and surprising comparison between two things that, at first glance, seem to have absolutely nothing in common. The writer takes an unexpected connection and stretches it out, develops it in detail, and makes it the backbone of the poem or passage. It's not a quick one-line simile. It's a comparison that the writer commits to, explores from multiple angles, and sustains throughout a piece of writing.

The key qualities of a conceit are:

  • It is surprising — you would not naturally think to compare these two things
  • It is clever and intellectual — it makes you think
  • It is extended — it is not just a flash of comparison but a developed, detailed argument built on that comparison

A famous example: The poet John Donne, in his poem "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning," compares two lovers — one about to go on a journey, one staying behind — to the two legs of a drawing compass (the instrument used to draw circles). This seems bizarre at first. What do lovers have to do with a compass? But Donne develops it fully: just as a compass has two legs joined at the top, the two lovers are spiritually joined. When one leg moves outward (one lover travels), the other leg (the one staying) leans toward it, remains anchored, and enables the moving leg to complete its circle and return to where it started. The further out one leg goes, the more the other leans with it. Donne uses every detail of how a compass actually works to describe the relationship between the lovers. That sustained, unlikely, intellectually worked-out comparison — that is a conceit.

The Two Types of Conceit You Should Know

1. The Petrarchan Conceit
Named after the Italian poet Petrarch, this type of conceit uses comparisons that, while elaborately developed, are conventional in love poetry — meaning they were used so often they became clichés. Comparing a woman's eyes to stars, her lips to red roses, her skin to snow, or her hair to rivers of gold — these are Petrarchan conceits. They were once considered beautiful and elevated, but over time they became so predictable that later writers mocked them. When Shakespeare wrote "My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun," he was deliberately pushing back against Petrarchan conceits.

2. The Metaphysical Conceit
This is the more intellectually daring and celebrated type. Associated with the Metaphysical poets of the 17th century (John Donne, George Herbert, Andrew Marvell), the metaphysical conceit reaches for shocking, unexpected, and often scientific or philosophical comparisons. The compass example above is a metaphysical conceit. These comparisons feel almost wrong at first — and then, as the poet develops them, they feel startlingly right. That tension between initial surprise and eventual sense is the hallmark of the metaphysical conceit.

Meaning 1Meaning 2

When you see "conceit" in an everyday sentence about a person's character or behavior, it means vanity and an inflated self-image.

When you see "conceit" in a sentence about a poem, a novel, a play, or writing in general, it means an extended, clever, and surprising comparison that structures a piece of writing.

These two meanings share the same word but nothing else. The literary term does not come from the idea of being proud; they simply evolved in the same language and arrived at the same spelling.

One final test to cement your understanding:

  • "His conceit made it impossible to work with him." → Pride. He thought too highly of himself.
  • "The central conceit of the poem is comparing grief to a slow tide coming in." → Literary device. The comparison between grief and a tide is the clever, extended metaphor that drives the poem.

Now you know everything there is to know about the noun "conceit" — both where it lives in daily life and where it lives in literature.
